head:
Act · Minimum effective dose

The minimum effective dose: how much, what, how often

Between “150 minutes a week”, “10,000 steps” and “a few minutes of intense effort is enough”, you could conclude that you need to give it your whole day or almost nothing. This article looks for the smallest dose the data justify, how to recognise it when you do it, and how to fit it into a real week, until you know what to do right now.

The problem

You have probably already received three pieces of advice that do not agree. Health authorities talk about 150 minutes a week. Your watch congratulates you at 10,000 steps. An article promises results from a few minutes of intense effort. Each has its own numbers, and nobody tells you which one is a minimum, which one is a target, or which one applies to your week.

The word “minimum” is itself a trap. It can mean a threshold below which nothing would happen, which the data do not show. It can mean the recommended dose, which is what the World Health Organization does. Or it can mean the smallest dose at which studies already see a difference, which is what the work on steps and on very brief efforts shows. These are three different answers, and they get mixed up in your head.

There is also a practical difficulty. Even with the right number, what do you count: an easy walk or a brisk one? One long session at the weekend or several short ones? And how do you check that you are doing it, without a laboratory?

The article “How much exercise to live longer” covers the other end of the subject: the full curve between dose and lifespan, and how far increasing the dose still helps. Here, we start from the bottom of the scale and ask what to keep when time is short.

The question

What is the smallest amount of activity that is worth doing, of what type and how often, and how do you know you are really reaching it?

We proceed in six steps, from the general framework to the detail: the official recommendation, how to measure intensity, what happens below the minimum, very brief efforts, how to condense or spread a week, then the objections. The answer comes next, followed by three typical weeks.

What is at stake

The first issue is collective, but it concerns you. According to the WHO, about 31% of adults, or 1.8 billion people, were not physically active enough in 2022, an increase of 5 points since 2010.2 The WHO adds that people who are insufficiently active have a 20 to 30% higher risk of death than people who are sufficiently active.2 This is an association between groups: it describes a population, not what will happen to you.

The second issue is the decision you make each week. If you believe that less than 150 minutes is useless, you may do nothing in the week when you have 60 available. If you believe that ten minutes of intensity replace everything, you may give up walking and strength training for a result that the data do not promise. Misreading the minimum costs time or energy.

The third issue is independence. For people aged 65 and over, the WHO guidelines do not talk only about endurance: they also ask for balance and strength. A minimum that took only cardio into account would be incomplete.1

The fourth is a measurement issue. Knowing that you need “moderate” effort does not help if you cannot recognise it. A minimum is only useful if it can be checked with what you have to hand: a stopwatch, how it feels, a step counter, and the test on this page. The question cannot be left unanswered: it decides how you divide up your time.

Step 1 of 6 · The general framework

The official recommendation is a window, not a threshold

We start with the reference text: the WHO 2020 guidelines, presented by their authors in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.1 For an adult aged 18 to 64, they ask for at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity endurance activity per week, or at least 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity, or an equivalent combination of the two. They also ask for muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that work all the major muscle groups, on at least 2 days a week.1

The 150 minutes are the bottom of a recommended window

Ranges published by the WHO for adults aged 18 to 64. The “vigorous converted into moderate minutes” line is a derived calculation: vigorous minutes multiplied by 2, which brings you back to the moderate range. The “additional benefits” beyond 300 moderate or 150 vigorous minutes are a conditional recommendation. Source: Bull et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020.1

What this means

The figure of 150 is the bottom of a recommended zone. It is not the border between “it helps” and “it does not help”: the WHO itself writes that any amount of activity is better than none.2 And one minute of vigorous effort counts for about two minutes of moderate effort, which is what the equivalence between the two ranges says. This is a conversion rule for reading, not an exact law.

Two details change the reading. First, the old rule that required periods of at least 10 minutes at a time has been removed: the authors write that activity counts whatever the duration of each period.1 Five minutes of brisk walking on the stairs and in the corridor therefore count towards the total. Second, the level of evidence is stated: the recommendations are rated “strong”, and for the weekly volumes of cardio and strength training they rest on evidence of broadly moderate certainty.1

For people aged 65 and over, the same endurance volumes apply. To these is added varied activity, which combines several types of effort and emphasises functional balance and strength, at moderate or greater intensity, on at least 3 days a week.1 For people with a chronic disease, the guidelines consider activity safe in the absence of contraindications, to be done according to one’s abilities.1 This article gives population benchmarks, not medical advice: if you have an illness, an injury or any doubt, a health professional adjusts the dose.

This framework rests on two words, “moderate” and “vigorous”. Before looking at what happens below the window, you need to know what they look like when you move.

Step 2 of 6 · Measurement

Recognising moderate or vigorous effort without a laboratory

The WHO defines intensity in two ways.1 The first is absolute and is expressed in METs. One MET is the energy expenditure of a person sitting at rest: an activity at 3 METs expends three times as much. Moderate effort runs from 3 METs up to less than 6. Vigorous effort starts at 6 METs. The second definition is relative, and depends on you: on a perceived exertion scale from 0 to 10, moderate is generally 5 or 6, vigorous 7 or 8.1

A feeling of 5 to 6 out of 10 corresponds to moderate, 7 to 8 to vigorous

Intensity definitions from WHO table 1. The values 0 to 4 and 9 to 10 are not detailed in the source read. Source: Bull et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020.1

What this means

METs tell you what type of activity is involved. How it feels tells you where you stand. The same brisk walk can be a 4 for a trained person and a 7 for someone returning to exercise: both therefore count together. The tool that costs nothing and adapts to your level on the day is the scale from 0 to 10.

A field benchmark complements this feeling, but it does not come from the documents read for this article, so take it as a coach’s habit, not a study result. At a moderate pace, you can hold a conversation in full sentences but you could not sing. At a vigorous pace, you can only say a few words at a time. This talk test serves to check your perceived effort, not to replace it.

For heart rate, we deliberately give no percentage: no source read here supports one, and your maximum heart rate is personal. If you wear a watch, look at the trend instead: at the same perceived effort, is your heart rate lower than two months ago?

For concrete anchors: in the Taiwanese study in the next step, participants classified their own activity into four categories: walking (light), brisk walking (moderate), jogging (vigorous) and running (very vigorous).7 This is a self-reported classification, so it is approximate: walking while chatting is not walking fast, and jogging is classed as vigorous.

It remains to be seen what doses that fall short of the window are worth.

Step 3 of 6 · The bottom of the scale

Below the minimum, the first steps already count

Two sets of work look at what happens when you do less than 150 minutes. The first counts minutes. A cohort of 416,175 Taiwanese adults, followed for 8 years on average, compared self-reported levels of leisure activity.7 The inactive, who reported less than one hour of activity per week and made up 54% of participants, serve as the reference. The lowest active level, 92 minutes per week, is associated with a 14% lower risk of all-cause death and about 3 more years of life expectancy. Each additional 15-minute increment is associated with a risk about 4% lower.7 The press release also writes “15 minutes a day” (which would make 105): we keep the 92 minutes, or about 60% of the WHO minimum (derived calculation).

The second set counts steps, which avoids having to remember what you did. A meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts followed 47,471 adults wearing a measuring device, with 3,013 deaths over a median follow-up of 7.1 years.3 Participants are split into four groups of equal size, whose median steps per day are 3,553, 5,801, 7,842 and 10,901. Compared with the first group, the risk of death is 0.60 for the second, 0.55 for the third and 0.47 for the fourth.3

Most of the gain comes before 6,000 steps, then it levels off earlier with age

All-cause risk of death, with the median group of 3,553 steps set at 1.00 (values 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47: published risk ratios). Levelling-off zones as published. The 10,000-step benchmark is described by the source as coming from a Japanese commercial campaign for pedometers. Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health, 2022, from a secondary report.3

What this means

Going from about 3,500 to about 5,800 steps a day is associated with a 40% lower risk (1 minus 0.60, derived calculation), which is most of the total drop, reaching 53% in the most active quarter (1 minus 0.47, derived). After age 60, the gain levels off between 6,000 and 8,000 steps, before 60 between 8,000 and 10,000.3 The 10,000 is therefore a round benchmark, not a threshold: you do not have to reach it for it to count.

Another study finds the same shape in a different population: 4,840 adults aged 40 and over from the American NHANES survey, fitted with an accelerometer for a week and followed for about ten years, with 1,165 deaths. Compared with a group at 4,000 steps a day, the group at 8,000 steps has a 50% lower risk of death, and the group at 12,000 steps a 65% lower risk.4 The authors add that walking speed adds nothing more once the total number of steps is taken into account.4 The meta-analysis qualifies this: the 30 most vigorous minutes of the day are associated with a risk ratio of 0.67.3 The role of walking intensity therefore remains debated, and volume is what can be asserted.

Minutes reported and steps measured by a device give the same shape. But they speak to people who walk, at least a little. What about those who have no sessions at all and do not plan any?

Step 4 of 6 · The very little

A few minutes of brief efforts scattered through the day are associated with a lower risk

The UK Biobank followed 25,241 people who reported doing no exercise, fitted with a wrist sensor, for 6.9 years on average, with 852 deaths.5 The sensor detected what the authors call vigorous intermittent lifestyle efforts, in short bursts: climbing stairs at a good pace or speeding up while carrying shopping are examples from the editorial text, not from the study text. At the median level of frequency, which is 3 efforts a day of 1 to 2 minutes, the publication page indicates a 38 to 40% lower risk of death (all-cause and cancer) and 48 to 49% (cardiovascular). At the median level of total duration, 4.4 minutes a day, the drop is 26 to 30% (all-cause and cancer) and 32 to 34% (cardiovascular).5

Three efforts of 1 to 2 minutes a day go with an already clear drop in risk

Drop in risk of death compared with no brief efforts, in 25,241 adults who do not exercise. The lighter part of each bar shows the published range. Source: Stamatakis et al., Nature Medicine, 2022, UK Biobank publication page (summary).5

What this means

In people who do no sessions at all, bursts of intensity lasting one to two minutes are associated with a notable difference. You should not conclude “4 minutes is enough”. What to take away is that intensity, even brief, is associated with a benefit in someone starting from zero, and that it can be obtained without changing your schedule. The page read is a summary: it gives neither the confidence intervals nor the limitations, and 852 deaths split across several causes is few. Those who produce these efforts may already be fitter and in better health.

We now have the shape of the bottom of the scale. What remains is the concrete problem of the week: the same dose can be spread in several ways, and available time is not regular.

Step 5 of 6 · Distribution

Condense or spread: one or two days, short intervals, strength training

Everything in one or two days. An analysis of two health surveys, English and Scottish, followed 63,591 adults with an average age close to 59, with 8,802 all-cause deaths, 2,780 cardiovascular and 2,526 from cancer (data from 1994 to 2012).8 The “weekend warriors”, who reach 150 moderate minutes or 75 vigorous in one or two sessions a week, have a risk of death about 30% lower than the inactive, 40% lower for cardiovascular deaths and 18% lower for cancer deaths.8 The press release specifies that the risk seems lower still in those who spread their activity regularly: concentrating keeps the essential without doing better. The activity was self-reported, more than 90% of participants were white and the study cannot establish causality.8

Short intervals for fitness. A meta-analysis of 53 randomised trials on 1,514 adults aged 19 to 47 compared high-intensity interval protocols for improving VO2max, the maximal oxygen capacity (see the article “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show”).6 In healthy adults, low-volume sessions (5 minutes or less, according to the authors’ definition) improve VO2max by 3.96 mL/kg/min compared with no training (interval from 2.73 to 5.18, six trials). Compared with continuous moderate training, these same sessions do neither better nor worse: the difference is 0.20 (interval from −1.53 to 1.94, seven trials). Short intervals of 30 seconds or less give 3.54 (1.85 to 5.23, three trials). Long intervals of 2 minutes or more give 7.62 (5.36 to 9.88, eight trials).6

Very short sessions improve fitness, without doing better than continuous moderate exercise

Mean difference in VO2max in healthy adults, with 95% confidence interval. VO2max expressed per kilo of body weight. Source: Wen et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2019 (table 1 of the article).6

What this means

To improve fitness, a few minutes of intervals work as well as continuous moderate exercise, and better than no training. The biggest gain nevertheless comes from long intervals and fuller sessions: the authors conclude that, to maximise the effect on VO2max, you need intervals of 2 minutes or more and sessions of 15 minutes or more.6 These results concern exercise capacity, not lifespan, and nothing in them indicates that five minutes of intervals replace walking or strength training.

Strength training, a separate dose. A meta-analysis of 16 cohorts shows that strength training alone is associated with an all-cause mortality risk of 0.85 (0.79 to 0.93; 7 studies, 263,058 participants), a cardiovascular risk of 0.83 and a diabetes risk of 0.83. For strength training combined with endurance, compared with neither, it is 0.60 (0.54 to 0.67; 3 studies).9 The dose associated with the lowest risk is about 40 minutes per week for all-cause mortality, 60 for cardiovascular disease and 30 for cancer, with a curve that rises again afterwards for these outcomes. The authors judge the certainty of this evidence “very low” for mortality.9 These benchmarks of 30 to 60 minutes should therefore be taken as an order of magnitude, and they should not be confused with the WHO instruction, which is expressed in days per week and not in minutes.1

It remains to examine what could distort this picture.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What can distort the demonstration, and what remains uncertain

Objection 1: healthier people move more

This is reverse causation. Someone who is ill, sometimes without knowing it, walks less and dies earlier, without the lack of activity being the cause. The authors of the American study on steps say so: the study is observational, it cannot prove that more activity reduces risk, and those who take many steps may already be in better health.4 In our reading (reasoning, not a result), this objection weighs more heavily on very low doses: someone who spontaneously speeds up several times a day may already be in good health to begin with.

Objection 2: we remember poorly what we do

The Taiwanese and British studies rely on questionnaires.7,8 The Taiwan study asks about activity in the previous month. The studies on steps and on brief efforts use a device, which avoids this bias. In the American study, it is worn for only one week, which represents a whole life poorly (the wearing period of the other studies is not stated on the pages read).

Objection 3: people were not drawn at random

None of the sources read here compares doses of activity on mortality at random. The article “How much exercise to live longer” covers the only randomised trial read on the subject, and it does not settle the question. The only randomised trials read in this article concern the improvement in VO2max (step 5), not lifespan.

Objection 4: small trials

The meta-analysis on intervals itself reports strong heterogeneity, possible publication bias and small trials. The short intervals rest on only three trials.6 These results give a direction, not an exact value for you.

Objection 5: what if it does not apply to me?

The cohorts read mostly concern middle-aged adults with an average age of about 59 to 62 where it is stated.5,8 The meta-analysis on intervals concerns ages 19 to 47.6 Steps are the only result read that distinguishes two age bands.3 For a person aged 20 or 80, these figures cannot be extended mechanically.

The answer to the problem

The question was: what is the smallest amount of activity that is worth doing, of what type, how often, and how do you know you are reaching it? Here is the answer, with the level of certainty of each piece.

What is solid. There is no threshold below which nothing happens: the WHO writes this, and all the studies read see a difference with doses below 150 minutes, whether activity is self-reported, counted in steps or measured by a sensor.2,3,4,7 The recommended target is a window of 150 to 300 moderate minutes or 75 to 150 vigorous, plus strength training on 2 days a week, with balance and strength on 3 days a week from age 65.1

What is probable. The first gains are the most worthwhile: about 92 minutes per week or about 5,800 steps per day are already associated with a clear difference.3,7 For those who do not have time to train, the total seems to matter more than the distribution, and brief efforts of intensity scattered through the day also go with a lower risk.5,8 To improve fitness, short intervals do as well as continuous moderate exercise.6

What remains uncertain. Whether the activity itself causes the difference, since everything comes from observations. The exact value of the smallest useful dose: the “4.4 minutes” or “92 minutes” are group benchmarks, not promises. The exact dose of strength training. The role of walking intensity. And what these averages mean for a specific person.

In one sentence: aim for the WHO window, but do not let the number serve as an excuse. Below the minimum, each minute remains associated with an advantage, and it is regularity, more than an exact figure, that builds the week.

What to put in place

The conversion of these results into a week is an editorial construction based on the studies, not a tested protocol. Equivalent minutes count one vigorous minute as two moderate minutes. Choose the profile that looks most like you.

Three typical weeks, from the starting point to an already vigorous level

Weeks built from the WHO benchmarks and the studies cited: they illustrate an order of magnitude and are not prescribed. Equivalent minutes are a derived calculation (vigorous times 2). The Beginner profile aims for 90 minutes, close to the 92-minute level of the Taiwanese study.1,7

Beginner: building the base
  • Three brisk 30-minute walks, two 15-minute strength sessions at home.
  • A week deliberately under 150 minutes, at the bottom of the scale in the studies (step 3). Then lengthen in steps of a few weeks.
  • Measure: your moderate minutes for the week (stopwatch), your perceived effort (5 to 6 out of 10 during the walks), whether you did your two strength sessions or not.
Irregular active: rescuing the week
  • One long moderate outing of 90 minutes, one vigorous session of 30 minutes, two 20-minute strength sessions, and three brief efforts of 1 to 2 minutes on quiet days.
  • Total of 150 equivalent minutes in two slots, like the “weekend warriors”. The brief efforts (step 4) are an editorial addition.
  • Measure: the number of weeks, out of four, in which you reach your total. Regularity is worth more than the peak.
Hybrid: staying in the window
  • Two moderate outings (45 and 90 minutes), one vigorous session of 30 minutes, two 30-minute strength sessions.
  • The total is about 195 equivalent minutes: within the window of 150 to 300. Nothing in the studies read indicates that you need to do more for longevity (see the article “How much exercise to live longer”).
  • Measure: the share of vigorous effort in your total (feeling of 7 to 8), your strength training volume, and how your test score changes.

In all three cases, the test on this page serves to place your current level and then to see whether your score moves. Do it once now, in conditions you can reproduce (same time of day, same warm-up, same surface), then repeat it every 8 to 12 weeks. This frequency is a coaching choice based on the length of the step 5 protocols, not a study finding. A difference from one week to the next may be nothing but measurement noise.

So, what do you do now? Here is the starting order, in four moves.

  1. Count one week without changing anything.Note your minutes of moderate or vigorous effort and your steps.
  2. Choose the closest profile, not the most ambitious.If you do less than 90 minutes, take the Beginner week. If you do most of it in one or two days, the Irregular active one. If you already reach 150 equivalent minutes, you are in the window.
  3. Put the slots in your calendar today.A slot fixed in advance is more likely to be kept than a session planned for “when I have time”. This is coaching advice, not a study result.
  4. Do the test on the page, then repeat it in 8 to 12 weeks.You will see whether your level has moved. If the result surprises you in a worrying way, or if you feel chest pain or abnormal breathlessness, seek medical advice before increasing the intensity.
What these figures do not say
  • All the relationships with mortality come from observational studies. Causality is not established.4
  • The typical weeks are editorial constructions. No study read has tested these precise weeks.
  • These population benchmarks do not replace personal medical advice, particularly in cases of illness, injury or pregnancy.1

Frequently asked questions

Do sessions need to be at least 10 minutes?

No. The WHO 2020 guidelines removed this rule: periods of any length count.1

Do you need to reach 10,000 steps?

No. The gain levels off between 6,000 and 8,000 steps after age 60, between 8,000 and 10,000 before, and the source describes this benchmark as coming from a commercial campaign.3

Do five minutes of intervals replace walking?

The data read do not say so. They show that very short sessions improve VO2max as much as continuous moderate exercise, but on exercise capacity, not on lifespan.6

What to do after 65?

The same endurance volumes, plus varied activity that works balance and strength, on at least 3 days a week, at moderate or greater intensity. In case of illness or doubt, ask a health professional for advice.1
